title: The Bumpy Tiles On The Sidewalk Are A Two-Word Language

scenes.narration: Those bumpy tiles at the edge of a train platform are a language, and it only has two words.
scenes.note: TONE: this is an accessibility feature, treated seriously. The comedy budget for this episode is zero.

beats.action: a yellow tactile strip runs along a platform edge; Bill stands beside it
the strip lights teal and the word LANGUAGE stamps beside it
two blank symbol cards slide in, waiting to be filled
the yellow strip runs on ahead down the length of the platform
beats.sync: secondary action — closes a pacing gap

scenes.narration: Round domes mean stop, because there is an edge, a road, or a drop ahead.
scenes.note: Symbol one. Domes fill the first card. The hazards are drawn as plain icons, not scenes of danger.

beats.action: a dome-pattern tile fills frame, drawn large
the first card fills with domes and stamps STOP
three small icons appear beside it — platform edge, kerb, stair
the dome pattern tilts slightly so the rows read in depth
beats.sync: secondary action — closes a pacing gap

scenes.narration: Long parallel bars mean keep going, this way is safe.
scenes.note: Symbol two, deliberately mirroring the previous scene so the pair reads as a set.

beats.action: a bar-pattern tile fills frame in the same framing as the domes
the second card fills with bars and stamps GO
a guiding path of bars draws forward across the floor

scenes.narration: Both are readable through a shoe or the tip of a cane, and the yellow helps if you still have some sight.
scenes.note: How it is actually read: through a sole, through a cane tip. Show contact, not a person struggling.

beats.action: a shoe sole meets the domes; the pattern registers up through it
a cane tip taps across the bars, each tap ringing a small mark
the tile colour saturates to high-contrast yellow against grey paving

scenes.narration: An engineer in Japan named Seiichi Miyake paid for the first ones himself in 1965, because a friend was going blind.
scenes.note: The origin. One man, his own money, one friend. Play it straight and let it land.

beats.action: a drafting desk; Gus sketches a dome tile by hand
the name and 1965 letter onto the drawing
a second figure is sketched beside the first at the drafting table; the two drawings sit together
the drawing is set down; a second sheet is squared beside it
beats.sync: secondary action — closes a pacing gap

scenes.narration: They are under most of the world's feet now.
scenes.note: Pull back and multiply. The scale IS the payoff. End on the tile, not on a face.

beats.action: the camera pulls back; tactile strips light up across street after street
the strips continue lighting to the horizon; hard cut
